PAPER: Journal of Financial Services Marketing (2026) 31:8 https://doi.org/10.1057/s41264-025-00337-4 ORIGINAL ARTICLE Sustained impact of higher customer satisfaction on bank revenue Carin Segerlind1 · Kent Eriksson2 · Cecilia Hermansson3 Received: 7 October 2024 / Revised: 26 October 2025 / Accepted: 16 November 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract This study examines the relationship between customer satisfaction and individual-level bank revenue growth, drawing on data from 19,060 Swedish retail banking customers that combine survey responses with objective bank records. Fur- thermore, we investigate whether the impact of satisfaction on revenue growth is sustained over time, specifically one, two three and four years after the measurement of satisfaction, and whether this effect differs across customer satisfaction levels. The results show that higher satisfaction is associated with greater sustained revenue growth, with more pronounced effects for customers in the medium-high and highest satisfaction groups. By contrast, no significant sustained revenue growth is found for customers with low and low-medium satisfaction. The findings do not support the hypothesis of dimin- ishing returns when moving from medium-high to the highest satisfaction levels, although weak indications suggest scope for further exploration. Overall, the findings demonstrate the long-term revenue growth of satisfied customers and empha- size the importance of targeting customers with lower to medium-low satisfaction to enhance overall revenue performance. JSON: Name: sustained_cs_revenue_pipeline Title: Longitudinal individual-level OLS and robustness analysis of the sustained effect of customer satisfaction on retail bank customer revenue growth Short Hypothesis: Higher customer satisfaction at time t causes greater individual customer revenue growth over the subsequent one to four years, controlling for demographic and financial covariates and base-year revenue. Related Work: Existing approaches examine the customer satisfaction (CS)–financial performance link at two scales: aggregate firm- or branch-level analyses and individual-customer cross-sectional studies. Firm-level work reports robust correlations between average CS and profitability but cannot isolate individual-level dynamics or sustained effects. Prior individual-level studies are limited by short horizons (commonly one to two years), sparse financial controls, and often rely on cross-sectional or simple lagged regressions, producing small or mixed effect sizes. Several studies note possible nonlinearity or threshold effects of CS on revenue but provide inconsistent empirical thresholds and limited tests for diminishing returns. Few prior analyses combine individual-level CS survey data with multi-year objective revenue records while controlling both demographic and customer financial context. Additionally, most work cannot allocate costs to customers, limiting conclusions about profit effects. Overall, unresolved issues include modest effect sizes, potential endogeneity, limited time horizons, and unclear nonlinear thresholds. Abstract: Problem: Determine whether customer satisfaction (CS) measured at the individual retail-banking customer level causally increases that customer’s revenue growth and whether that effect persists for up to four years and varies across satisfaction levels. Approach: Use a longitudinal, customer-level pipeline that links a one-time CS survey to objective bank-recorded revenue (interest and fees) for 19,060 customers across 2013–2017. Estimate OLS growth regressions using base-year revenue and a set of demographic and financial covariates, compare categorical and continuous CS specifications, and run robustness checks (quadratic terms, quantile regressions, propensity-score matched samples, clustered and bootstrapped standard errors). Contribution: Provide an individual-level, multi-year estimate of CS effects on subsequent revenue growth while testing nonlinearity and sustained effects up to four years and quantifying sensitivity to demographic and financial controls. Expected outcome: Produce statistically characterized estimates of short- and medium-term revenue effects attributable to CS, identify whether medium-high or highest CS levels drive revenue gains, and delineate the limits of causal inference given observational data. Experiments: Data: 19,060 retail customers from a single Swedish retail bank; CS measured via three 1–10 items converted to 0–100 index in base year 2013; objective customer revenue (CR) defined as annual sum of interest and provision fees for 2013–2017; control variables: age, gender, base-year CR (2013), total savings, total loans, net monthly salary; exclude negative-CR outliers as in source. Primary estimands: OLS coefficient of CS on percent growth in CR from 2013 to 2014, 2013 to 2015, 2013 to 2016, and 2013 to 2017. Baselines and model suite: (A) Unadjusted OLS: percent CR growth ~ CS_category dummies (0–49,50–69,70–84,85–100); (B) Demographics-adjusted: add age and gender; (C) Financial-adjusted: add base CR, savings, loans, salary; (D) Continuous CS: replace dummies with continuous CS index; (E) Nonlinearity: include quadratic CS term and test threshold dummies; (F) Aggregated baseline: replicate firm-level aggregated regression for comparability; (G) Matching: propensity score matching on demographics and financials to estimate average treatment effect of moving between CS groups (50–69 vs 70–84 and 70–84 vs 85–100); (H) Quantile regressions at 25th, 50th, 75th percentiles of CR growth; (I) Robustness: cluster standard errors by branch, bootstrap 1,000 samples, and winsorize CR-growth at 1%/99% to test sensitivity. Ablation studies: remove base-year CR to quantify bias; remove financial controls to quantify omitted-variable impact. Evaluation metrics: estimated coefficients and 95% confidence intervals, p-values with multiple-testing correction (Benjamini–Hochberg), adjusted R-squared and AIC/BIC for model fit, average treatment effect estimates for matching with bootstrap CIs, change in explained variance from ablation. Reported outputs: per-year treatment effect estimates (percentage-point CR growth), model diagnostics, and robustness tables for all variations. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sample and generalizability: single-country (Sweden) and single-bank sample limits external validity to other banking systems, customer mixes, or regulatory environments. Measurement: CS measured at one point in time; absence of repeated CS measures prevents modeling within-customer CS change; objective revenue excludes cost allocation so profitability cannot be assessed. Endogeneity: possible reverse causality (higher prior revenue influences reported CS) and omitted-variable bias (unobserved customer financial wealth, outside-bank relationships, macro shocks) threaten causal interpretation. Statistical: small effect sizes may be statistically significant but economically marginal; CR distribution non-normal with heavy tails and outliers may bias OLS estimates despite winsorization. Instrumentation: no credible instrument available in provided data, limiting causal identification to robustness and matching approaches. Operational: limited control over measurement error in survey responses and potential non-response or survival bias from customers leaving the bank. Computation and scalability: analyses are modest computationally but advanced causal methods requiring external instruments or granular cost data are not feasible with current dataset.
